title: The good question
hookLine: in the study hall a sharp question earns more respect than a quick answer

lines: DID YOU ASK A GOOD QUESTION?
cards: Other kids came home from school, the story goes, and their mothers asked: what did you learn today? Isidor Rabi's mother asked something else. Izzy, did you ask a good question today?
Rabi grew up in a Jewish immigrant family in New York and became a Nobel Prize-winning physicist. He said that question made him a scientist.
People often tell this story, and whether every detail happened just that way, nobody can check. It keeps getting retold because it fits the study hall so well.
There, the person everyone turns to isn't the one with the fastest answer. It's the one who says: wait. That doesn't make sense.

teach.h: THE MISHNAH OPENS WITH A QUESTION.
teach.b: Open the Mishnah, the early rabbinic collection of Jewish law, to its very first line. It doesn't start with a rule. It starts with a question: from what time may the Shema be said in the evening?
The whole Talmud grows from there, and page after page, its engine is the question.

teach.h: KUSHYA: A DIFFICULTY, SAID OUT LOUD.
teach.b: The Aramaic word is kushya, a difficulty. A student notices two verses that seem to disagree, or a rule that doesn't fit, and says so. The Talmud doesn't hide these.
It lines them up and works on them, sometimes for pages.
Sometimes the answer never comes, and the Talmud says so plainly: teiku, let it stand. Some later readers heard in that word a hope that Elijah the prophet would one day come and settle it.
Until then, the question stays on the table, honored.
The rabbis also taught, in Pirkei Avot, that a shy person can't learn: someone too embarrassed to ask stays where they are.

And every year at the Passover seder, a child, often the youngest, asks: why is this night different from all other nights? The Haggadah tells the story of the Exodus as an answer to a child's question.
So what makes a question good? It's real: you actually want to know.
It's close to the text: it points at a word, not a vague feeling. And it's brave: it risks sounding like you missed something. A quick answer ends the conversation.

how: In Jewish study, students are expected to raise difficulties with the text out loud, and the Talmud records unresolved questions rather than hiding them; at the Passover seder, children ask the Four Questions.

o: a hard question raised about a text
a rule everyone must follow without asking
a quick answer that settles a debate

games.q: questions in the study hall — tap the pairs.
p: when may the Shema be said at night?

s: the Mishnah opens with a rule
it opens with a question: from what time may the evening Shema be said?
the Talmud sometimes leaves a question unanswered
teiku: let it stand. the question stays on the table.
Pirkei Avot praises the student too shy to ask

games.q: you're new in the study hall. the teacher reads a line that seems to contradict one from last week. what do you do?
o: stay quiet so you don't look slow.
say it out loud: these two don't fit.
assume you misremembered and move on.
games.why: you raise it. a kushya, a difficulty said out loud, is how the Talmud moves, and a shy person, Avot says, can't learn.

practice: Think of something you've been told so often you stopped asking about it: a rule at work, a family habit, a line you've heard all your life.
Ask one honest question about it, not a complaint, but a question you'd actually like answered. Turn it until it's sharp and short.

wordCard.voice: Kushya. A difficulty: the Aramaic word for the hard question that, in the study hall, earns more respect than a quick answer.

orig.note: Aramaic: a difficulty, the hard question the Talmud raises and works on.

carryVoice: Your line: ask better. In the study hall, the hard question is the honored one. Day one hundred fifty-two, done.
